The compound-angle identities express a trigonometric function of a sum or difference using values at the two component angles.
Setting one angle to a familiar value produces cofunction and reference-angle identities; setting the angles equal produces double-angle formulas.

items.text: The sine and cosine identities hold for all real angles.
The tangent identity requires every tangent shown and the quotient denominator to be defined; verify the original tangent at the compound angle as well.
The upper signs form the addition formula and the lower signs form the subtraction formula.

runs.text: The result follows by substituting the exact sine and cosine values for 45 and 30 degrees into the addition formula.

items.text: Cosine uses the opposite sign in its cross term; sine uses the same sign as the compound angle.
There is no identity that distributes sine or cosine over addition.
A simplified tangent quotient may hide angles where an intermediate tangent is undefined.
